name: Bali-Vitu, Bali dialect
catalog_citation: Ross, Malcolm. 2002. Bali-Vitu. In John Lynch, Malcolm Ross & Terry Crowley (eds.), The Oceanic Languages (Curzon Language Family Series), 362-386. Richmond: Curzon.
catalog_locator: p. 363, section 1.3 'Stress' (pdf page 380 of the saved scan; page rendered to image and read); dialect statement p. 362 (pdf page 379)
catalog_quote: Stress is penultimate. This means that in words where Bali retains an erstwhile final consonant with a following echo vowel but Vitu loses the consonant, stress falls on different syllables in the two dialects: e.g. Bali /kau'aka/, Vitu /'kaua/ 'dog'; Bali /βo'roto/, Vitu /'βoro/ 'sun'. However, stress is most obvious in citation forms. In continuous speech, vowels tend to be of roughly equal length, suggesting that Bali-Vitu is a syllable-timed language.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (941 pp, text layer; archive.org item crowley-.-the-oceanic-languages) plus the chapter extract. I rendered pdf pages 379-380 (book pp. 362-363) to images and read them directly. On p.363, section '1.3 Stress' reads exactly: 'Stress is penultimate. This means that in words where Bali retains an erstwhile final consonant with a following echo vowel but Vitu loses the consonant, stress falls on different syllables in the two dialects: e.g. Bali /kau'aka/, Vitu /'kaua/ 'dog'; Bali /βo'roto/, Vitu /'βoro/ 'sun'. However, stress is most obvious in citation forms. In continuous speech, vowels tend to be of roughly equal length, suggesting that Bali-Vitu is a syllable-timed language.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; because Bali (Uneapa) keeps historical final consonants plus an echo vowel, the penult (and hence the stress) is one syllable later than in the Vitu cognate.
new_statements.exceptions: None as such; author notes stress is clearest in citation forms and that connected speech sounds syllable-timed with vowels of roughly equal length. Sec. 1.4 notes optional clitic-final vowel loss (bali=taza -> [baltaza]) creating surface CVC syllables, without comment on stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement illustrated with citation forms; author explicitly contrasts citation forms (stress obvious) with continuous speech (less obvious). Description is of the Bali (Uneapa) dialect, data from a speaker of Ketinerave village.
new_statements.identity_note: Ross 2002 treats Bali and Vitu as two dialects of one language 'Bali-Vitu' but states (p.362) 'The description here is of Bali' (Unea Island, vernacular Uniapa = Uneapa, unea1237), with Vitu (mudu1242) mentioned only contrastively; the stress statement is therefore first-hand for Uneapa. The Vitu OPD already held under mudu1242 independently gives penultimate stress for Vitu.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on placement: the catalog (penult, from Ross 2002 p. 363 on Bali) and van den Berg & Bachet 2006 (penult, on Vitu) agree; Ross 1988 is silent. One analytic difference between the two descriptions: van den Berg & Bachet count every vowel as a syllable and therefore describe 'kaua 'dog' as antepenult-stressed with a stress-shift rule for au/ai/ou/oi sequences, whereas they note that Ross 2002:363 treats such sequences as diphthongs for Bali (so the same forms are penult-stressed under his syllabification). This is a syllabification convention, not a different stress system, and it is stated for Vitu, not Bali.
